arc.summary: Flight 370 takes its name from the airliner that vanished in 2014 and borrows that one image: something gone without a trace. Across twelve songs he's lost in different ways, grieving someone who died, watching a relationship come apart and seeing friends turn on each other, with flexes and love songs in between. The last stretch climbs toward hope, and the closer claims the whole record as R&B.

tracks.1: Takeoff in anger: a friend turns on him over a girl.
tracks.2: Grief arrives: a song for someone he lost, with The Part Time Models.
tracks.3: A detour into lust and bravado, offering to take her on the road.
tracks.4: Lost on purpose: he'd vanish into the Bermuda Triangle if she came.
tracks.5: The softest stop, a love song built on Clairo's bedroom pop.
tracks.6: Friends turn on one of their own, with The Part Time Models.
tracks.7: Bravado in gold chains and cartoon jokes, ending on a proposal image.
tracks.8: The relationship starts sinking: arguments, baseball metaphors and the Titanic.
tracks.9: A warm spell: he falls hard and brings her home to the beach.
tracks.10: Letting go: he ends it, though her shadow stays, with The Part Time Models.
tracks.11: The past haunts him, then the light turns into hope.
tracks.12: The landing: a plea for closeness, and he claims the record as R&B.

notes.body: The album opens with him talking. He addresses a guy who's been running his mouth over a girl SyWavy walked away from, and tells him he should be grateful instead. On a record about loss, the hurt shows up first as attitude.

Crashing out is slang for losing your temper and acting without thinking. On an album named for a plane that vanished, the slang doubles as the first crash, and he says the whole crew has already gone down.

notes.title: Do the Right Thing
notes.body: Spike Lee's 1989 film about one scorching day on a Brooklyn block that boils over. Buggin' Out is one of its characters, so the line pairs the title with his name to say everyone is losing their cool.
The chorus is about what was done to him. By the outro he turns the same words around, and the people who crossed him are the ones left lost and hurting.

The opening verse is a confession to a partner. He owns up to messing with her head and to a fling he says meant nothing, then asks where the two of them actually stand, a question that closes every section of the song.

The hook holds two losses at once: a couple who drifted apart, and a death that can't be undone. The garden of the title is where they meet, with flowers for someone who deserved them and tears falling like rain to water them.

notes.title: Mojo Jojo
notes.body: The chimp villain of The Powerpuff Girls, who got his powers from the same Chemical X accident that made the girls. He splits the name in two to say her love gave him powers of his own.

The second verse is the album's first goodbye. He hears through a friend that someone he lost loved his music, and the news lands in the middle of memories that still feel ordinary and close. He ends wishing the song could reach them, which makes the whole track a message that can't be delivered.

notes.title: No Change
notes.body: His own song from the 2020 EP Ear Candi. This song's hook echoes its title, and here he ties that older song to someone he lost.

notes.title: Ding dong ditch
notes.body: The prank of ringing a doorbell and running before anyone answers. He flips the words around in a run of memories.
Touring means two things here: chasing someone and being on the road. He's hooked on her and can't have her, and the hook ends with him crying, which says more than the bragging around it.

notes.title: Magic City
notes.body: Atlanta's best-known strip club, open since 1985 and famous in hip-hop for breaking hit records. Naming it puts her on its stage.

notes.title: A Milli
notes.body: Lil Wayne's 2008 single, built on one word looped over and over. He picks up the chant right after talking about a million dollars.

notes.title: Tha Carter III
notes.body: Lil Wayne's 2008 album, one of the best-selling hip-hop records of its decade and the home of A Milli.

notes.title: Barter 6
notes.body: Young Thug's 2015 mixtape, first announced as Carter 6 in a nod to Lil Wayne that turned into a public feud. Pairing the two titles sets up the next line, which plays on Young Thug's name.

The chorus swaps roles back and forth. He asks to come along on her journey, then offers to bring her on his and show her everything is hers to have. It's the most generous moment in the album's opening stretch.

The last verse runs on rhymes that sound alike but come from different places: a body part, the back of a book, a website and a word about money. It's playful, and it ends with him asking her to be his date on the road.

notes.title: Pinterest
notes.body: The site people use to collect outfit and decor ideas. The jab is that her look came straight off someone else's board.

notes.title: Shake Weight
notes.body: A vibrating dumbbell sold on late-night TV around 2010 that became a running joke for how its two-handed workout looked.

notes.title: Malaysia Airlines Flight 370
notes.body: The Malaysia Airlines flight that disappeared over the Indian Ocean in March 2014 with 239 people aboard; its main wreckage has never been found. The album borrows only its name and the image of something vanishing, and here he signs the song with the album's title.

notes.title: Bermuda Triangle
notes.body: The stretch of the Atlantic between Miami, Bermuda and Puerto Rico, famous for stories of ships and planes vanishing. On an album named for a missing plane, it's where he wants to get lost with her.
An artifact is something rare that's been dug up and kept. Calling her one says she's a find worth holding onto, his first choice over anyone else.

notes.title: H-E-double-hockey-sticks
notes.body: The playground way of spelling out hell without saying it. He's just called her heaven-sent, so there's none of the other place here, and the hockey sticks set up the hockey joke in the next lines.

notes.title: Patrick Bateman
notes.body: The Wall Street killer at the center of American Psycho, Bret Easton Ellis's 1991 novel and the 2000 film with Christian Bale. He swaps in his state and his own names for the title and the character.

notes.title: Jason Statham
notes.body: The British action star, whose 2012 thriller Safe has him protecting a young girl from the people hunting her. He's the first of two Jasons in a row, both rhymed off Bateman.

notes.title: Jason Bateman
notes.body: The actor who played Marty Byrde in Netflix's Ozark, a financial planner who gets pulled into washing dirty money. The line borrows that role, and the name rhymes back to Patrick Bateman two lines up.
The bridge turns the album's crash imagery into a plea. Like a castaway sending out a distress call, he's asking her not to go.

notes.title: SOS
notes.body: The Morse code distress signal, often said to stand for a plea to save souls. Sending one fits an album named for a missing plane.

The Bermuda Triangle becomes a pun on trying new angles with her. Then he flips the album's main image: he'd board a plane that disappears, as long as she disappears with him. Like any prized artifact, she's something to put on the wall and keep.

notes.title: Atlanta
notes.body: Atlanta, Georgia. He opens by calling out the city, which is also where Clairo was born.

notes.title: Clairo
notes.body: The singer-songwriter Claire Cottrill, born in Atlanta, who broke out in 2017 with Pretty Girl, a song she filmed in her bedroom. The song borrows her name and the bedroom pop sound she's known for.

The song is a love letter built from Clairo's world. Her birthplace, her debut album and its lead single, and later her breakout song all show up as ways to describe his girl, so another artist's catalog becomes his vocabulary for how he feels.

notes.title: Immunity
notes.body: Clairo's 2019 debut album. He calls his girl the queen of it, keeping the song inside Clairo's world.

notes.title: Bags
notes.body: The lead single from Clairo's Immunity. He borrows the title for the moment she drops her bags at his place.

notes.title: Bedroom pop
notes.body: Soft, close-up pop recorded at home on simple gear, with Clairo as one of its best-known names. He turns the genre's name into a double meaning about what happens in his room.
The middle is the most tender stretch on the album. He wants her close and at home, and by the end the ask shrinks to one thing: stay with him.

notes.title: Pretty Girl
notes.body: Clairo's 2017 breakout, a lo-fi song with a webcam video that went viral. He keeps working the title into his lines about his girl.

notes.title: Hi-Chew
notes.body: A chewy fruit candy from Japan. Said aloud it sounds like a sneeze, and a sneeze gets a blessing, which is the joke.

The spoken intro frames it as a final flight: a whole group ganged up to freeze out one of their own, and he can't make sense of it. Some people leave and some people cry, he says. He does both, and the tears are for the others.

From here the song turns into a street story told in quick pieces, about people who were supposed to be trusted and weren't. The repeated boast about coming out ahead lands hard against the tears of the intro.

notes.title: Jett2Fly
notes.body: Jett2Fly is SyWavy's producer and creative partner. The line turns his name into a verb for flying home fast.

notes.title: St. Petersburg, Florida
notes.body: Locals call St. Pete the Burg. Seeing the Burg in someone means seeing his hometown in them, for better or worse.

notes.title: The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker
notes.body: Nintendo's 2002 sailing adventure, whose cartoon-style hero fans call Toon Link. He splits the title into waking her up, and the hero's name sets up the link in the next line.

ref.name: The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker

notes.title: Cuban link chain
notes.body: The thick, tightly woven chain that's a staple of hip-hop jewelry. He jokes that his Cuban talks in Spanish, then plays on link as in meeting up.

The chorus pulls the album's water imagery into a flex song: she loses herself in him like something swept out to sea. He can't take his eyes off her jewelry, and the section ends with him ready to get down on one knee and offer a ring of his own.

notes.title: Logan's Roadhouse
notes.body: The steakhouse chain famous for free buckets of peanuts on every table, which is where the line's joke lands.

notes.title: Hulk Hogan
notes.body: The wrestling star, a longtime Clearwater resident, whose WWE contract was cut in 2015 after a leaked recording of him objecting, in racist language, to his daughter dating a Black man. The line pokes right at that.
He says out loud that he's switching his voice, then says he's switching back a few lines later, so the verse plays like two characters trading lines. In between, he names himself after the song.

notes.title: Tasmanian Devil
notes.body: Taz, the spinning, wild-eyed Looney Tunes character. Between the cartoon's name and Taz's stare, he paints her as going wild for him.

The song opens in the middle of an argument. He's tired of being blamed and of trying to fix her doubts, and says he had to step back for his own sake. He doesn't want to leave, but he no longer feels safe staying.

notes.title: Chicago White Sox
notes.body: The Chicago baseball club. He names both Sox teams and slides into base in one line, starting a baseball thread that runs to the end of the song.

notes.title: Boston Red Sox
notes.body: The Boston baseball club, paired with the White Sox in the same line to set up the song's talk of bases and being safe.
Break keeps changing meaning: a breakthrough he's tired of chasing, a break she wants from him, and breaking up for good. Under the wordplay is a simple complaint: he can't understand her anymore.

notes.title: Titanic
notes.body: The ocean liner that sank on its first voyage in 1912. The relationship is the ship here, and he's afraid it's going down.
The baseball thread pays off. A runner who reaches a base is called safe, and by the last line there's no base left, so there's nowhere safe for the two of them to land.
Melting is the whole idea: falling for someone so hard he loses his shape. His heart skips and races, and he can't stop wanting more of her.

notes.title: Wu-Tang Clan
notes.body: The Staten Island group behind the 1993 album Enter the Wu-Tang (36 Chambers). He name-checks them, then borrows one of their best-known hooks.

notes.title: C.R.E.A.M.
notes.body: Wu-Tang Clan's 1994 single, its title an acronym for a line about money ruling everything. The ad-libs chant it while he leans on the other meaning of cream.
For a moment the album touches down at home. He brings her to his city, she falls for the beach, and he's taken with the way she talks.

notes.title: Boy Meets World
notes.body: The 1990s ABC sitcom about Cory Matthews growing up, with Topanga as the girl he loves from childhood and later marries. He puts his own name in the title and casts his girl as his Topanga.

He steps outside the song at the end, admits he can't always explain it himself, and names the album out loud. Then he puts it plainly and tells her he loves her. On a record about losing people, it's a moment of holding on.
She's gone, but she still follows him the way a shadow does, a dark outline of someone who isn't there anymore. That's why goodbye won't come easily.

notes.title: Shadow the Hedgehog
notes.body: Sega's 2005 game starring Sonic's dark rival, who, unusually for the series, carries guns. The line borrows that image for his crew.
The hook works the physics of light: walk toward it and your shadow falls behind you. So asking her to stay back means two things at once: keep trailing me, and let me go on without you.

This is the plainest writing on the album. He admits he isn't sure it was ever love, that the two of them weren't built to last, and that he can't wait any longer to tell her. He'll miss her and he'll look back, and he leaves anyway.
He opens by talking and sets this song apart from the rest: the past keeps coming back on him, and making music is how he handles it.

notes.title: X
notes.body: The social network once called Twitter. She's there now, quietly watching what he posts.
The title borrows a horror story about a haunting, but the hook moves from haunted to hopeful. Shining becomes light, and all he asks is that she glow and belong to him.

notes.title: The Shining
notes.body: Stephen King's 1977 novel and Stanley Kubrick's 1980 film about a family snowed in at a haunted hotel. The song takes the title and the haunting, then turns shining into light and hope.

notes.title: The Part Time Models
notes.body: A group SyWavy works with, featured on three Flight 370 songs, Botanical Gardens, Catch Flights & CRY and Shadows, and later on the 2025 single Put It On!. The line plays on their name, as if modeling were a side job that pays well.
This is where the album turns toward hope. He's learned how little he really knew, but hearing her love him back is enough, and she brightens every one of his days.

notes.title: Burning sage
notes.body: Burning sage, often called smudging, is a ritual for clearing a space of bad energy. He credits her with doing that for him at his worst.

12.title: Can't Tell Me What It's Not

notes.body: The last song opens with a spoken warning to anyone who says this isn't R&B. After a record full of singing and heartbreak, he settles the genre question himself, and the title is the same dare.

notes.title: Devin Haney
notes.body: The American boxer and former undisputed lightweight champion. Getting knocked out leads straight to his name, which also rhymes with baby.

notes.title: Fugees
notes.body: The trio of Lauryn Hill, Wyclef Jean and Pras, whose 1996 album The Score includes Ready or Not. He works their name and that song title into the same line.

notes.title: India Love
notes.body: The model and social media personality. Her name sounds like the next line's confession, which swaps her out for the person he's actually fallen for.

notes.title: LUT
notes.body: In video editing, a LUT is a preset that sets the color and mood of footage. SyWavy also directs, and he asks for more of her the way an editor reaches for a favorite look.

notes.title: The Sandlot
notes.body: The 1993 movie about a summer of neighborhood baseball, where Squints famously chases a lifeguard far out of his league. The league line points at both.
The refrain asks her to keep him near for as long as she's around. An album that began with people turning away ends with a request for closeness.

notes.title: Groot
notes.body: The walking tree from Marvel's Guardians of the Galaxy. Tree is slang for weed, so his name stands in for what they rolled.

notes.title: DeBarge
notes.body: The Motown family group led by El DeBarge, behind 1980s ballads like All This Love. Naming them on this song backs up its claim to R&B.

notes.title: La Liga
notes.body: Spain's top soccer league, home of FC Barcelona and Real Madrid. It's another league joke after the Sandlot line: his team isn't one they can join.
